summary: The article argues that Christmas carols, rather than commercial holiday songs, convey the true message that love triumphs over hate amid war and suffering. It centers on Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's Christmas Day 1863 poem "I Heard the Bells on Christmas Day," written during the Civil War and personal tragedy, and draws parallels to today's wars in Israel and Ukraine. It also notes the poem is the subject of the film "I Heard the Bells" and concludes that God's love is stronger than hate.
one_line: Using Longfellow's Civil War-era poem and Christmas carols, the article argues God's love triumphs over hate, war and suffering.
key_facts: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote "I Heard the Bells on Christmas Day" in 1863, exactly 160 years before the article.
In 1863 the Civil War was raging, a war that would claim nearly a million lives.
Longfellow's wife Fanny, married 18 years and mother of his six children, died in a fiery accident when her dress caught fire from a lit candle.
Longfellow's son Charlie was critically injured fighting for the Union army near Washington, D.C.
Each stanza of Longfellow's poem ends with "peace on Earth, good will to men," a phrase based on the King James translation of Luke 2:14 and referring to humanity, not the male gender.
The poem moves from joyful bells to despair ("There is no peace on earth") and ends with bells declaring "God is not dead, nor doth He sleep; The Wrong shall fail, The Right prevail."
The author laments that advertisers use carols for marketing, such as a phone company's radio ad using "Joy to the World" to hype a new phone plan.

"Carol of the Bells" is the most popular Christmas carol used in marketing ads; according to GodTube its biblical inspiration has Old Testament roots, including Zechariah 14:20, Exodus 28:33-35 and Psalm 150.
The author says carols like "What Child Is This" and "O come O come Emanuel" hold joy and sorrow together, including the sorrow that Jesus was born to die.
Emanuel means "God with us," which the author says brought a new, category-busting power into the world.
The story of the poem is the subject of a feature-length film, "I Heard the Bells," available on demand through most cable and streaming platforms.
Columnist Cal Thomas said, "You can change hairstyles, clothes, styles, modes of transportation... But nothing really seems to change … A lot of that has to do with human nature."
